title: The borrowed colt (Mark 11:1–11)
hook: the Lord has need of it: the entry into Jerusalem on an unridden colt
carry: the lord has need of it
tomorrow: the fig tree and the temple

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bartimaeus shouted louder and was asked a plain question. Your line was what do you want? Did you answer someone honestly? Day two hundred six.

Imagine two strangers walking up to your car in the driveway, untying it, well, unlocking it, and starting to drive off. You'd run out. What are you doing? And they say one sentence, and you let them go. That's roughly what happens here. Jesus and his friends reach the Mount of Olives, just outside Jerusalem. He sends two of them into the village ahead: you'll find a colt tied up that no one has ever ridden. Untie it and bring it. And if anyone asks why, in the King James Bible, "say ye that the Lord hath need of him; and straightway he will send him hither." So they go. It's there, tied by a door in the street. People standing by ask: what are you doing, untying that colt? They give the answer. And the people let them go.
screen: `AT THE MOUNT OF OLIVES.` → `UNTIE IT AND BRING IT.` → `THE LORD HATH NEED OF HIM.`

segments.voice: Who owned the colt? Mark doesn't say. A friend, maybe, or someone who'd been told ahead; the text is silent. What it keeps is the loan: someone let go of something valuable, on a single sentence, because the Lord had need of it. Then the scene everyone knows. They throw their cloaks on the colt, and Jesus sits on it. People spread their cloaks on the road, and others cut leafy branches from the fields. Notice Mark doesn't say palms. That detail comes from John's Gospel, and it's where Palm Sunday gets its name. And the crowd shouts: "Hosanna; Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord." Hosanna comes from Hebrew, and it means something like save, please. By then it had also become a shout of praise. The words come from Psalm 118, a psalm pilgrims sang on the way up to the temple. Why a colt, and not a warhorse? Matthew and John quote the prophet Zechariah: your king comes to you, humble, riding on a donkey. Mark doesn't quote it, but many readers hear it anyway. A king, but not the kind who arrives on a stallion. And then the ending, which only Mark tells like this. After all the shouting, he goes into the temple, looks around at everything, and since it's late, walks back out to Bethany with the twelve. No speech. Just a long look. Christians remember this day as Palm Sunday, the start of Holy Week, and in many churches people carry palms or branches and sing hosanna.
screen: `WHO OWNED IT? MARK IS SILENT.` · `CLOAKS AND LEAFY BRANCHES.` · `HOSANNA: SAVE, PLEASE.` · `A LONG LOOK, THEN BETHANY.` · then, large: `BLESSED IS HE THAT COMETH IN THE NAME OF THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find something to lend freely. Settle, and breathe. Picture the things you keep tied up by your own front door. Your car. Your tools. Your good pan. Your time on Saturday. Your spare room. Who could use one of them? Picture untying it and letting it go, no fuss, no conditions, trusting it to come back. Notice what makes you hesitate, and be gentle with that. If you pray, you can offer what you have to God's use. The bell holds the time.
The borrowed colt. Lent on one sentence, never ridden before, carrying a humble king into Jerusalem.
Your line: the lord has need of it. Today, lend something freely to someone who needs it, and don't make them ask twice. Day two hundred six.

howItsDone: Christians remember this entry on Palm Sunday, the start of Holy Week; in many churches people carry palm branches in procession and sing hosanna, and the palms are sometimes kept and later burned for the next year's Ash Wednesday.

fork.setup: you're standing by a doorway when two strangers untie a young colt. you ask what they're doing. they say: the Lord hath need of him. what do you do?
options: stop them until the owner comes.
fork.reveal: the bystanders let them go. one sentence, and a valuable animal is lent freely.

original.note: Greek spelling of a Hebrew cry: save, please. from Psalm 118:25.

trapdoor: what you thought: a parade with palm branches.
what it means: a king arriving humbly on a borrowed colt, greeted with hosanna, who ends the day with a long, quiet look at the temple.
what a scholar hears: hosanna from Psalm 118:25, save, please; Zechariah 9:9 is quoted by Matthew and John, not Mark; palms are John's detail.

sources.quoted: say ye that the Lord hath need of him; and straightway he will send him hither.

notes: Hosanna: from Hebrew hoshi'a na, 'save, please', which by the first century was also used as an acclamation; confirm.
Psalm 118 as a pilgrim/Hallel psalm sung on the way to the temple; confirm phrasing.
Mark's pōlos is usually understood as a young donkey (as Matthew and John have), though the word alone can mean a young horse; the script avoids the question.
howItsDone: burning the previous year's palms for Ash Wednesday ashes is a Catholic and some Anglican/Lutheran custom; confirm 'sometimes'.
